'''bairn''' (bãrn), ''n.'' [Sc. form of the reg. E. ''barn''<sup>2</sup> (now only dial.), < ME. ''barn'', ''bern'', < AS. ''bearn'' (= OS. ''barn'' = OFries. ''barn'' = OD. ''baren'' = OHG. MHG. ''barn'' = Icel. Sw. Dan. ''barn'' = Goth. ''barn''), a child, < ''beran'', E. ''bear''<sup>1</sup>.] A child; a son or daughter. See ''barn''<sup>2</sup>. [North. Eng. and Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Think, like good Christians, on your ''bairns'' and wives.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}
As she annunciated to her ''bairns'' the upshot of her practical experience, she pulled from her pocket the portions of tape which showed the length and breadth of the various rooms at the hospital house. {{right|''Trollope.''}}}}
'''Bairns’ part of gear.''' {{smaller|In ''Scots law'', same as ''legitim''.}}

'''bairnliness''' (bãrn′li-nes), ''n.'' [< *''bairnly'' (< ''bairn'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>) + ''-ness''.] Childishness; the state of being a child or like a child. [Scotch.]

'''bairntime''' (bãrn′tīm), ''n.'' [Sc., < ME. ''barn-team'', ''barn-tem'', etc., < AS. ''bearn-teám'' (= OFries. ''barn-tām''), a family, < ''bearn'', child, bairn, + ''teám'', family: see ''bairn'' and ''team''.] A family of children. [Old Eng. and Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Thae bonnie ''bairntime'' Heav’n has lent.
{{right|''Burns'', A Dream.}}}}

'''bairnwort''' (bãrn′wėrt), ''n.'' A name for the common English daisy, ''Bellis perennis''.

'''baisemain†''' (bāz′mān), ''n.'' [F., < ''baiser'', kiss (< L. ''basiare'', kiss, < ''basium'', a kiss), + ''main'', < L. ''manus'', hand.] A kissing of the hands; in the plural, compliments; respects. ''Spenser.''

'''baisement†''', ''n.'' Same as ''baisemain''.

'''bajadere''', ''n.'' See ''bayadere''.

'''bajdarka''', ''n.'' Same as ''bidarkee''.

'''Bajimont’s Roll.''' See ''Bagimont’s Roll'', under ''roll''.

''bājra'' or ''bājri'', also ''bājrā''; ''bājri'' prop. denotes a smaller kind, which ripens earlier.] A species of millet, ''Pennisetum typhoideum'', much used in the East Indies, especially for feeding cattle and horses.

''bacchan'', MHG. ''bachen'', G. ''backen'' = Icel. ''baka'' = Sw. ''baka'' = Dan. ''bage'', bake, prob. = Gr. φώγειν, roast, parch.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To

'''bakehouse''' (bāk′hous), ''n.'' [E. dial. also ''backhouse''; < ME. ''bak-house'', ''bachouse'' (= LG. ''backhus''), < AS. ''bæchūs'', < ''bacan'', bake, + ''hūs'', house.] A building or an apartment used for the preparing and baking of bread, etc.

'''bake-meat†''', ''n.'' See ''baked-meat''.

'''baken†''' (bā′kn). An obsolete past participle of ''bake''.

'''baker''' (bā′kėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''baker'', ''bakere'', < AS. ''bæcere'' (= OS. ''bakkeri'' = D. ''bakker'' = G. ''bäcker'', ''becker'' = Icel. ''bakari'' = Sw. ''bagare'' = Dan. ''bager''), < ''bacan'', bake: see ''bake'' and ''-er''<sup>1</sup>. Hence ''bakester'', ''backster''<sup>1</sup>, ''baxter''.] '''1.''' One who bakes; specifically, one whose business it is to make bread, biscuit, etc.—'''2.''' A small portable tin oven used in baking. [U. S.]—'''3.''' The popular name of the flesh-fly, ''Sarcophaga carnaria''.—{{smaller|'''Bakers’ dozen''', thirteen reckoned as a dozen. It was customary for bakers, like some other tradesmen, to give 13 for 12, the extra piece being called among bakers the ''in-bread'' or ''to-bread''. Brewer says the custom originated when heavy penalties were inflicted for short weights, bakers giving the extra bread to secure themselves.—'''Bakers’ itch''', a species of psoriasis, so called when it is confined to the back of the hand. It often appears in bakers.—'''Bakers’ salt''', subcarbonate of ammonia, or smelling-salts, so called from its being used by bakers as a substitute for yeast in the manufacture of some of the finer kinds of bread.}}

'''baker-foot''' (bā′kėr-fu̇t), ''n.''; pl. ''baker-feet'' (-fēt). [Cf. ''baker-legged''.] An ill-shaped or distorted foot: as, “bow-legs and ''baker-feet'',” ''Jer. Taylor'' (?), Artif. Handsomeness (1662), p. 79.

'''baker-kneed''' (bā′kėr-nēd), ''a.'' Same as ''baker-legged''.

'''baker-legged''' (bā′kėr-legd), ''a.'' Disfigured by having crooked legs, or legs that bend inward at the knees.

'''bakery''' (bā′kėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''bakeries'' (-iz). [< ''bake'' + ''-ery''.] '''1.''' The trade of a baker. [Rare.] —'''2.''' A place used for making bread, etc., or for the sale of bakers’ goods; a bakehouse or baker’s establishment; a baker’s shop.

'''bakester†''', ''n.'' [Also ''backster'', ''baxter'' (whence the proper name ''Baxter''), < ME. ''bakestere'', ''bacster'', ''baxter'', usually masc., < AS. ''bæcestre'' (fem. in form, but masc. in use), a baker, < ''bacan'', bake, + ''-es-tre'', E. ''-ster''.] A baker; properly, a female baker: as, “brewesteres and ''bakesteres'',” ''Piers Plowman''. In Scotland commonly written ''baxter'': as, ''baxter'' wives.

'''bakestone''' (bāk′stōn), ''n.'' [E. dial., also ''backstone''.] A flat stone or slate on which cakes are baked. [Prov. Eng.]

'''bakey''' (bā′ki), ''n.'' [Sc., also ''bakie'' and ''baikie'', dim. of ''back''<sup>3</sup>, ''n.''] A square wooden vessel, narrower at the bottom than at the top, and with a handle on each of two opposite sides, used for carrying coals, ashes, etc.; a wooden coal-scuttle. Also spelled ''bakie'' and ''baikie''. See ''back''<sup>3</sup>, 3. [Scotch.]

''barn''<sup>2</sup> (now only dial.), < ME. ''barn'', ''bern'', < AS. ''bearn'' (= OS. ''barn'' = OFries. ''barn'' = OD. ''baren'' = OHG. MHG. ''barn'' = Icel. Sw. Dan. ''barn'' = Goth. ''barn''), a child, < ''beran'', E. ''bear''<sup>1</sup>.]   A child; a son or daughter. See ''barn''<sup>2</sup>. [North. Eng. and Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Think, like good Christians, on your ''bairns'' and wives.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
{{smaller block|As she annunciated to her ''bairns'' the upshot of her practical experience, she pulled from her pocket the portions of tape which showed the length and breadth of the various rooms at the hospital house. {{right|''Trollope.''}}}}
'''Bairns’ part of gear.''' {{smaller|In ''Scots law'', same as ''legitim''.}}

'''bairnliness''' (bãrn′li-nes), ''n.''   [< *''bairnly'' (< ''bairn'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>) + ''-ness''.]   Childishness; the state of being a child or like a child. [Scotch.]

'''bairntime''' (bãrn′tīm), ''n.''   [Sc., < ME. ''barn-team'', ''barn-tem'', etc., < AS. ''bearn-teám'' (= OFries. ''barn-tām''), a family, < ''bearn'', child, bairn, + ''teám'', family: see ''bairn'' and ''team''.]   A family of children. [Old Eng. and Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Thae bonnie ''bairntime'' Heav’n has lent.
{{right|''Burns'', A Dream.}}}}

'''bairnwort''' (bãrn′wėrt), ''n.'' A name for the common English daisy, ''Bellis perennis''.

'''baisemain†''' (bāz′mān), ''n.''   [F., < ''baiser'', kiss (< L. ''basiare'', kiss, < ''basium'', a kiss), + ''main'', < L. ''manus'', hand.]   A kissing of the hands; in the plural, compliments; respects.   ''Spenser.''

'''baisement†''', ''n.'' Same as ''baisemain''.

'''bait'''<sup>1</sup> (bāt), ''v.''   [< ME. ''baiten'', ''beiten'', ''bayten'', ''beyten'' (= OF. ''beter'', bait, in comp. ''abeter'', urge on, abet, > E. ''abet'', q. v.), < Icel. ''beita'', feed, hunt, as with hounds or hawks, bait, as a hook (= Sw. ''beta'' = Dan. ''bede'', bait, = AS. ''bǣtan'', also ''gebǣtan'', bridle, curb (cf. ''bātian'', bait, < ''bāt'', bait), = MD. ''beeten'' = OHG. ''beizen'', ''beizzen'', MHG. G. ''beizen'', bait), lit. cause to bite, < ''bīta'' = AS. ''bītan'', E. ''bite'': see ''bite''. In senses 5 and 6 the verb is from the noun. Cf. ''bate''<sup>5</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To cause to bite; set on (a dog) to bite or worry (another animal).—'''2.''' To provoke and harass by setting on dogs; set a dog or dogs to worry or fight with for sport, as an animal that is hampered or confined: as, to ''bait'' a bull or a bear.
{{smaller block|We’ll ''bait'' thy bears to death. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., v. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' To set upon, as a dog upon a captive animal; hence, to harass in any way; annoy; nag; badger; worry.
{{smaller block|<poem>As chained beare whom cruell dogs doe ''bait''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. xii. 35.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>How oft have I been ''baited'' by these peers,
And dare not be revenged.</poem>
{{right|''Marlowe'', Edward II., ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Baited'' thus to vexation, I assum’d
A dulness of simplicity. {{right|''Ford'', Fancies, iv. 2.}}</poem>}}
'''4.''' To feed; give a portion of food and drink to, especially upon a journey: as, to ''bait'' horses.
{{smaller block|<poem>The Sunne, that measures heaven all day long,
At night doth ''baite'' his steedes the Ocean waves emong.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. i. 32.}}}}
'''5.''' To put a bait on or in: as, to ''bait'' a hook, line, snare, or trap.

{{smaller block|Many sorts of fishes feed upon insects, as is well known to anglers, who ''bait'' their hooks with them.
{{right|''Ray.''}}}}
'''6†.''' To allure by a bait; catch; captivate: as, “to ''bait'' fish,” ''Shak.'', M. of V., iii. 1.
{{smaller block|<poem>Do their gay vestments his affections ''bait?''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But this day she ''baited''
A stranger, a grave knight, with her loose eyes.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, iv. 2.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To act in a worrying or harassing manner.—'''2.''' To take food; feed.—'''3.''' To stop at an inn, while on a journey, to feed the horses, or for rest and refreshment.
{{smaller block|Thence ''baiting'' at Newmarket, stepping in at Audley End to see that house againe, I slept at Bishops Strotford, and the next day home.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Sept. 13, 1677.}}}}

'''bait'''<sup>1</sup> (bāt), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bait'', ''bayte'', ''beite'', ''beyte'', < Icel. ''beita'', f., bait (cf. ''beit'', neut., a pasture), (= AS. ''bāt'', bait, = MHG. ''beiz'', ''beize'', hunting), < ''beita'', feed, bait: see the verb. The E. noun is in part directly from the E. verb.]   '''1.''' Any substance, as an attractive morsel of food, placed on a hook or in a trap to allure fish or other animals to swallow the hook or to enter the trap, and thereby be caught; specifically, worms, small fishes, etc., used in fishing. Hence —'''2.''' An allurement; enticement; temptation.
{{smaller block|<poem>I do not like that ring from him to her,
I mean to women of her way; such tokens
Rather appear as ''baits'' than royal bounties.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Their riper years were knowne to be unmov’d with the ''baits'' of preferment.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}
{{smaller block|The chief ''bait'' which attracted a needy sycophant to the court was the hope of obtaining, as the reward of servility and flattery, a royal letter to an heiress. {{right|''Macaulay.''}}}}
'''3.''' A portion of food and drink; a slight or informal repast. (''a'') Refreshment taken on a journey, by man or beast.
{{smaller block|If you grow dry before you end your business, pray take a ''bait'' here: I’ve a fresh hogshead for you. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Scornful Lady.}}}}
(''b'') A luncheon; food eaten by a laborer during his shift. [Prov. Eng.] —'''4.''' A halt for refreshment or rest in the course of a journey.
{{smaller block|The tediousness of a two hours’ ''bait'' at Petty France, in which there was nothing to be done but to eat without being hungry, and loiter about without anything to see, next followed. {{right|''Jane Austen'', Northanger Abbey, p. 123.}}}}
'''5†.''' A refreshment or refresher.
{{smaller block|A pleasaunt companion is a ''bait'' in a journy. {{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 198.}}}}
'''6†.''' A hasty meal; a snack.
{{smaller block|He rather took a ''bait'' than made a meal at the inns of court, whilst he studied the laws therein. {{right|''Fuller'', Worthies (ed. 1840), II. 507. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}
'''7.''' Short for ''whitebait.''

'''bait<sup>2</sup>†''', etc. An obsolete form of ''bate''<sup>1</sup>, etc.

'''bait-box''' (bāt′boks), ''n.'' '''1.''' A small box in which anglers carry worms or small bait for fish.—'''2.''' A tank in which bait for fish is taken to the fishing-ground.

'''baiter''' (bā′tėr), ''n.'' One who baits or worries (animals); hence, a tormentor; a tease.

'''baith''' (bāth), ''a.'', ''pron.'', or ''conj.'' A Scotch form of ''both.''

'''baiting''' (bā′ting), ''n.''   [< ME. ''baiting'', ''bayting'', etc.: verbal n. of ''bait''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' The act of worrying a chained or confined animal with dogs. Hence —'''2.''' The act of worrying and harassing; persistent annoyance.—'''3.''' The act of halting on a journey for rest and food for either man or beast.—'''4.''' The act of furnishing a trap, hook, etc., with bait.

'''bait-mill''' (bāt′mil), ''n.'' A mill used by American fishermen for cutting mackerel, salted herrings, etc., into small pieces for bait. {{smaller|It consists of a roller armed with knives and inclosed in an upright wooden box, and is worked by a crank on the outside.}}

'''bait-poke''' (bāt′pōk), ''n.'' In ''coal-mining'', the bag in which bait or luncheon is carried into the mine.

'''baittle''' (bā′tl), ''a.'' A Scotch form of ''battle''<sup>3</sup>.

'''baitylos''', ''n.'' See ''bætylus''.

'''baize''' (bāz), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''bays'', ''bayes'', ''bease'', ''baies'', < OF. ''baies'' (Godefroy), pl., also in sing. ''baye'' (Cotgrave), baize (whence also D. ''baai'', LG. ''baje'' (> G. ''boi'') = Sw. ''boj'' = Dan. ''baj'' = Russ. ''baika'', baize; cf. dim. Sp. ''bayeta'' = Pg. ''baeta'' = It. ''bajetta'', baize), < ''bai'' (= Sp. ''bayo'' = Pg. ''baio'' = It. ''bajo''), bay-colored. The word is thus prop. pl. of ''bay''<sup>6</sup>, formerly used also in the singular: see ''bay''<sup>6</sup>.]   '''1.''' A coarse woolen stuff with a nap on one side, and dyed in plain colors, usually red or green. {{smaller|Baize (or bay) was first manufactured in England in 1561, under letters patent issued to certain refugees from the Netherlands, who had settled at Sandwich and other places and were skilled in weaving. Baize is now chiefly used for linings, table-covers, curtains, etc.; but when first introduced it was a much thinner and finer material, and was used for clothing. See ''bay''<sup>6</sup>.}} '''2.''' Any article, as a table-cover, a curtain, etc., made of baize; specifically, in theaters, the plain curtain lowered at the end of a play.

'''baize''' (bāz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''baized'', ppr. ''baizing''.   [< ''baize'', ''n.'']   To cover or line with baize.

'''bajadere''', ''n.'' See ''bayadere''.

'''bajdarka''', ''n.'' Same as ''bidarkee''.

'''Bajimont’s Roll.''' See ''Bagimont’s Roll'', under ''roll''.

'''bajjerkeit''' (baj′ėr-kīt), ''n.''   [< Beng. ''bajrakit'' (Hunter).]   A name of the ''Manis pentadactyla'' or scaly ant-eater, an edentate mammal of Africa.

'''bajocco''', ''n.'' See ''baiocco''.

'''bajra'''<sup>1</sup> (buj′rä), ''n.''   [Hind. and Beng. ''bajrā''.]   Same as ''budgero''.

'''bajra'''<sup>2</sup>, '''bajri''' (baj′rä, -rē), ''n.''   [Also written ''bajree'', ''bajeree'', ''bajury'', repr. Hind. ''bājra'' or ''bājri'', also ''bājrā''; ''bājri'' prop. denotes a smaller kind, which ripens earlier.]   A species of millet, ''Pennisetum typhoideum'', much used in the East Indies, especially for feeding cattle and horses.

'''bajulate†''' (baj′ū-lāt), ''v. t.''   [< L. ''bajulatus'', pp. of ''bajulare'', bear a burden: see ''bail''<sup>2</sup>.]   To carry to some other place, as in badgering (which see).

'''bake''' (bāk), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''baked'', ppr. ''baking''.   [< ME. ''baken'', < AS. ''bacan'' (pret. ''bōc'', pp. ''bacen'') = D. ''bakken'' = LG. ''bakken'' = Fries. ''backe'' = OHG. ''bacchan'', MHG. ''bachen'', G. ''backen'' = Icel. ''baka'' = Sw. ''baka'' = Dan. ''bage'', bake, prob. = Gr. φώγειν, roast, parch.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cook by dry heat in a closed place, such as an oven: primarily used of this manner of cooking bread, but afterward applied to potatoes, apples, etc., and also flesh and fish: to be distinguished from ''roast'' (which see).
{{smaller block|I have ''baked'' bread upon the coals. {{right|Isa. xliv. 19.}}}}
'''2.''' To harden by heat, either in an oven, kiln, or furnace, or by the sun’s heat: as, to ''bake'' bricks or pottery.—'''3†.''' To harden by cold.
{{smaller block|They ''bake'' their sides upon the cold hard stone.
{{right|''Spenser.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The earth
When it is ''bak’d'' with frost.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To do the work of baking.
{{smaller block|I keep his house; and I wash, wring, brew, ''bake'', . . . and do all myself. {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' To undergo the process of baking.

'''bake''' (bāk), ''n.''   [< ''bake'', ''v.'' Cf. ''batch''<sup>1</sup>.]   A baking.
{{smaller block|After this Esau finished the oven, and accomplished a ''bake'' of bread therein. {{right|''Three in Norway'', p. 126.}}}}

'''bakeboard''' (bāk′bōrd), ''n.'' A board on which dough is kneaded and rolled out in making bread.

'''baked-apple''' (bākt′ap′l), ''n.'' A name given in Labrador to the dried fruit of the ''Rubus Chamæmorus'', or cloudberry.

'''baked-meat†''', '''bake-meat†''' (bākt′-, bāk′mēt), ''n.''   [Prop. ''baked meat''; < ''baked'' + ''meat''.]   '''1.''' Food prepared by baking; a dish of baked meat or food.
{{smaller block|In the uppermost basket there was of all manner of ''bake-meats'' for Pharaoh. {{right|Gen. xl. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thrift, thrift, Horatio! the funeral ''bak’d meats'' Did coldly furnish forth the marriage tables.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' A meat-pie.
{{smaller block|<poem>You speak as if a man
Should know what fowl is coffin’d in a ''bak’d-meat''
Afore you cut it up.</poem>
{{right|''Webster'', White Devil, iv. 1.}}}}

'''bakehouse''' (bāk′hous), ''n.''   [E. dial. also ''backhouse''; < ME. ''bak-house'', ''bachouse'' (= LG. ''backhus''), < AS. ''bæchūs'', < ''bacan'', bake, + ''hūs'', house.]   A building or an apartment used for the preparing and baking of bread, etc.

''bager''), < ''bacan'', bake: see ''bake'' and ''-er''<sup>1</sup>. Hence ''bakester'', ''backster''<sup>1</sup>, ''baxter''.]   '''1.''' One who bakes; specifically, one whose business it is to make bread, biscuit, etc.—'''2.''' A small portable tin oven used in baking. [U. S.]—'''3.''' The popular name of the flesh-fly, ''Sarcophaga carnaria''.—{{smaller|'''Bakers’ dozen''', thirteen reckoned as a dozen. It was customary for bakers, like some other tradesmen, to give 13 for 12, the extra piece being called among bakers the ''in-bread'' or ''to-bread''. Brewer says the custom originated when heavy penalties were inflicted for short weights, bakers giving the extra bread to secure themselves.—'''Bakers’ itch''', a species of psoriasis, so called when it is confined to the back of the hand. It often appears in bakers.—'''Bakers’ salt''', subcarbonate of ammonia, or smelling-salts, so called from its being used by bakers as a substitute for yeast in the manufacture of some of the finer kinds of bread.}}

'''baker-foot''' (bā′kėr-fu̇t), ''n.''; pl. ''baker-feet'' (-fēt).   [Cf. ''baker-legged''.]   An ill-shaped or distorted foot: as, “bow-legs and ''baker-feet'',” ''Jer. Taylor'' (?), Artif. Handsomeness (1662), p. 79.

'''baker-kneed''' (bā′kėr-nēd), ''a.'' Same as ''baker-legged''.

'''baker-legged''' (bā′kėr-legd), ''a.'' Disfigured by having crooked legs, or legs that bend inward at the knees.

'''bakery''' (bā′kėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''bakeries'' (-iz).   [< ''bake'' + ''-ery''.]   '''1.''' The trade of a baker. [Rare.] —'''2.''' A place used for making bread, etc., or for the sale of bakers’ goods; a bakehouse or baker’s establishment; a baker’s shop.

'''bakester†''', ''n.''   [Also ''backster'', ''baxter'' (whence the proper name ''Baxter''), < ME. ''bakestere'', ''bacster'', ''baxter'', usually masc., < AS. ''bæcestre'' (fem. in form, but masc. in use), a baker, < ''bacan'', bake, + ''-es-tre'', E. ''-ster''.]   A baker; properly, a female baker: as, “brewesteres and ''bakesteres'',” ''Piers Plowman''. In Scotland commonly written ''baxter'': as, ''baxter'' wives.

'''bakestone''' (bāk′stōn), ''n.''   [E. dial., also ''backstone''.]   A flat stone or slate on which cakes are baked. [Prov. Eng.]

'''bakey''' (bā′ki), ''n.''   [Sc., also ''bakie'' and ''baikie'', dim. of ''back''<sup>3</sup>, ''n.'']   A square wooden vessel, narrower at the bottom than at the top, and with a handle on each of two opposite sides, used for carrying coals, ashes, etc.; a wooden coal-scuttle. Also spelled ''bakie'' and ''baikie''. See ''back''<sup>3</sup>, 3. [Scotch.]<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
